parole.significato: Any of the North American flowering plants of the genus Camassia.
parole.testo: Perhaps from Chinook Jargon qamaš, qawaš (“camas”), from Nootka qawaš (“camas”), or perhaps from Nez Perce qém̓es (“camas”).

parole.significato: Someone new to Alaska or the Yukon; originally, a gold rush newcomer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinook Jargon cheechako.

parole.significato: Synonym of chum salmon.
parole.testo: From Chinook Jargon tzum (“spotted, marked”), from Chinook.

parole.significato: A salmon species, Oncorhynchus keta.
parole.testo: From Chinook Jargon tzum (“spotted, marked”) (from Chinook) + English salmon.

parole.significato: To go; depart, leave.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinook Jargon tlatoa (“to go”), from Nootka ƛatw̕a (“to paddle away”).

parole.significato: Synonym of lingcod (Ophiodon elongatus).
parole.testo: From Chinook Jargon cultus (“worthless, of little worth”), probably from a Chinook word kaltas/kə́ltas ("only", "in vain").

parole.significato: Synonym of candlefish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinook Jargon ulakan, from Clatsop Chinook.

parole.significato: Beads or shells, especially as placed on strings and valued as ornaments or a sort of currency.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinook Jargon hywka, hyakwa, from Nootka.

parole.significato: A person in a position of power, authority, or status.
parole.testo: From Chinook Jargon hiyu muckamuck (“plenty of food”). Compare muckamuck.

parole.significato: A type of fish, an anadromous smelt, Thaleichthys pacificus, found in the North Pacific.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinook Jargon ulakan, from Clatsop Chinook, with spelling and pronunciation influenced by the preceding.

parole.significato: The shell of Antalis pretiosa, formerly used as money and ornaments (hiaqua) by Native American and Aboriginal people o…
parole.testo: A variant of hiaqua, from Chinook Jargon, from Nootka.

parole.significato: Synonym of quiggly hole.
parole.testo: From Chinook Jargon keekwillie (“under”).

parole.significato: Any member of a Native American tribe formerly living along the Klamath River in California and Oregon.
parole.testo: From Chinook Jargon Tlamatl (“either "swiftness" or "they of the river"”), with the first syllable's onset consonant cluster dissimilated and the coda of the second syllable changed to the somewhat similar-sounding interdental fricative during the process of anglicization.

parole.significato: Woman, wife (especially if Native American).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinook Jargon, from Nootka, see below.

parole.significato: A plant or herb with edible roots, in the genus Lomatium, used in traditional Native American foods and medicines.
parole.testo: From Chinook Jargon.

parole.significato: A person in a position of power or authority, or of high status.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinook Jargon muckamuck (“food”). In the sense of person of authority, it is short for high muckamuck, from Chinook Jargon hayo muckamuck (“plenty to eat, plenty of food; to eat”). See muckety muck. parole.significato: A ceremony amongst certain indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest in which gifts are bestowed upon guests and pers…
parole.testo: The noun is borrowed from Chinook Jargon potlatch, pátlač (“to give; gift; gift-giving ceremony, potlatch”), from Nootka Jargon pa'chatle, pa'chēētle, pah-chilt (“to give, give me”), from Nootka p̕ačiƛ (“to give a gift during a potlatch ceremony”). parole.significato: Synonym of quiggly hole.
parole.testo: From Chinook Jargon keekwillie (“under”).

parole.significato: The remains of a pithouse or earth lodge made by First Nations people in the interior regions of the Pacific Northwest.
parole.testo: From Chinook Jargon keekwillie (“under”) + hole.

parole.significato: Oncorhynchus tshawytscha, the chinook salmon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinook Jargon equan'nat, itself borrowed from Chinook ikʷanat.

parole.significato: A leathery-leaved North American shrub, Gaultheria shallon, with edible sepals and leaves.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinook Jargon from Chinook.

parole.significato: Any body of saltwater, especially the ocean.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinook Jargon saltchuck (“the sea”, literally “saltwater”), from salt (“salt”) (from English salt) + chuck (“water”) from Nootka č̕aʔak (“water”).

parole.significato: A Native American.
parole.testo: Chinook Jargon siwash

parole.significato: Excellent, impressive.
parole.testo: First attested in 1825–35. Borrowed from Chinook Jargon, from Lower Chehalis.

parole.significato: A variety of deciduous shrub (Shepherdia canadensis), the Canadian buffaloberry, the red fruit/berries of which may be…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Chinook Jargon, from soop (“soap”) (from English) + olallie, ollalie (“berry”) (from a Kwak'wala or Chinook word for berries). Compare soapberry.

parole.significato: A remote, rural area; a place that is removed from civilization such as the boondocks.
parole.testo: Possibly derived from 1800s Chinook Jargon stick (“tree, forest”), from English stick.

parole.significato: Broadleaf arrowhead (Sagittaria latifolia), or its edible bulbous root.
parole.testo: From Chinook Jargon wapato, from Wasco-Wishram, or a word from an unknown Algonquian language used by the Lewis and Clark expedition.

parole.significato: A talk; talking; a meeting or conversation.
parole.testo: From Chinook Jargon wawa.
